1 OurBigBook.com
A branch point is a point around which analytic continuation changes the value of a multivalued function. For z1/2=r1/2eiθ/2, one circuit around zero changes the sign. A branch cut removes paths producing this ambiguity; for example −π<argz<π gives a single holomorphic square root off the nonpositive real axis. The position of a cut is a convention, while the branch point is intrinsic.
Set q(z)=(z−1)/(z+1). For z outside the closed segment joining −1 to 1, q(z) avoids the nonpositive real axis. Therefore the principal square root of q defines a holomorphic function there, with the normalization f(∞)=1. The endpoints are branch points. Expanding at infinity,
f(z)=(1−z+12​)1/2=1−z1​+O(z−2).
(1)
For a positively oriented contour surrounding the cut, its integral equals the integral on a sufficiently large positively oriented circle, since the intervening annulus is holomorphic. Thus
IΓ​=−2πi.​
(2)
On the upper and lower banks, f+​(x)=+i(1−x)/(1+x)​ and f−​(x)=−i(1−x)/(1+x)​. The upper bank is traversed from 1 to −1, and the lower bank from −1 to 1. Their sum is −2i times the required real integral. Small endpoint arcs vanish because their singularities have exponent less than one. Consequently
∫−11​1+x1−x​​dx=π.​
(3)
For α=1/n, use fα​=qα with the same normalization. Its expansion is 1−2α/z+O(z−2), and its bank values are e±iπα[(1−x)/(1+x)]α. Equating the contour integral −4πiα with −2isin(πα) times the real integral gives
∫−11​(1+x1−x​)1/ndx=nsin(π/n)2π​.​
(4)
The condition n≥2 ensures endpoint integrability. Choosing the other square-root branch reverses IΓ​, but also reverses both bank values, leaving the real integral unchanged.

Solution
Words: 90
a OurBigBook.com
Integrate eiz/z around an upper semicircle, indenting the origin by a small upper semicircle traversed clockwise. The integrand is holomorphic inside the indented contour. The large arc vanishes by Jordan's lemma, and the small arc contributes −iπ, so
PV∫−∞∞​xeix​dx=iπ.
(5)
Taking imaginary and real parts yields
∫−∞∞​xsinx​dx=π,PV∫−∞∞​xcosx​dx=0.​
(6)
The first integrand has a removable singularity at zero and its tails converge conditionally by Dirichlet test for improper integrals. The second integral needs a principal value at zero; its zero also follows from oddness with symmetric exclusion. One must not assign an ordinary convergent integral to its singularity.

Words: 53
b OurBigBook.com
Put z=eiθ, so sinθ=(z−z−1)/(2i) and dθ=dz/(iz). The integral becomes
∮∣z∣=1​6z2+13iz−6dz​.
(7)
The poles are −2i/3 and −3i/2; only the first is inside the unit circle. The derivative of the denominator there is 12(−2i/3)+13i=5i. The residue theorem therefore gives
∫02π​13+12sinθdθ​=52π​.​
(8)
There are no poles on the contour because the real denominator is at least one.

Solution

Words: 264
3 OurBigBook.com
At a regular point, f(z0​+ζ)−f(z0​)=f′(z0​)ζ+O(ζ2). Multiplication by a nonzero complex number rotates every tangent by the same angle and multiplies every length by the same positive factor. Oriented angles are preserved. If the first derivative vanishes but the second does not, the leading term is f′′(z0​)ζ2/2: tangent arguments are doubled, so angles are doubled, modulo the identification of rays. This is a local statement; holomorphy alone does not imply global injectivity.
Write z=x+iy. Then
w=sin2πx​cosh2πy​+icos2πx​sinh2πy​.
(9)
For −1<x<1 and y>0, the imaginary part is positive. The bottom edge maps monotonically to [−1,1]; the left and right vertical edges map to (−∞,−1] and [1,∞) respectively. The inverse below establishes that every point of the open upper half-plane occurs exactly once. At fixed y=a, putting u=Rew, v=Imw, one obtains
cosh2(πa/2)u2​+sinh2(πa/2)v2​=1,v≥0.​
(10)
This is the upper half of an ellipse, traversed from its left endpoint to its right endpoint.
Choose the branch s(w)=1−w2​ analytic in the upper half-plane and positive on the boundary interval (−1,1). Then the inverse branch into the strip is
z=−π2i​log(iw+s(w)).​
(11)
The logarithm is chosen continuously so that −1<Rez<1 and Imz>0; for instance w=iv, v>0, gives z=(2i/π)arsinhv. Differentiation gives dz/dw=2/(π1−w2​). The only zeros of the original derivative in the closed strip are z=±1, with images w=±1. The inverse has square-root branch points there, and cannot extend holomorphically across them. At either corner the original map doubles the right angle to a straight angle; a holomorphic inverse with nonzero derivative could not halve it. The open strip interior has no such failure.

a OurBigBook.com
The distance modulus at 100pc is five magnitudes. Thus the two approximate main-sequence endpoints read from the original figure, mV​≃0,20, correspond to MV​≃−5,15. With the given solar reference,
LV,⊙​LV​​=10−0.4(MV​−5)≃104,10−4.
(12)
Use the figure's approximate endpoint effective temperatures 25,000 K and 2500 K. If V-band luminosity is used as a rough bolometric proxy, the Stefan–Boltzmann law gives
R⊙​R∗​​≃(L⊙​L​)1/2(Teff​T⊙​​)2.
(13)
Taking T⊙​≃5800 K gives
Rsmall​≃0.054R⊙​,Rlarge​≃5.4R⊙​.​
(14)
These are schematic estimates, not precision radii. The diagram supplies V magnitudes rather than bolometric luminosities, and hot and cool endpoints need different bolometric corrections. The exact range cannot be recovered without those corrections; the quoted values state the intended approximation explicitly.

Words: 136
b OurBigBook.com
Integrating dP/dr=−GMr​ρ/r2 in order of magnitude, with ρ∼M∗​/R∗3​, gives
Pc​∼R∗4​GM∗2​​.
(15)
The ideal gas law independently gives Pc​∼M∗​kB​Tc​/(μmH​R∗3​). Equating the two estimates yields
R∗​∼kB​Tc​GμmH​​M∗​.​
(16)
For similar composition and an approximately fixed hydrogen-burning central temperature, R∗​∝M∗​. Calibrating this rough relation on the Sun and using part a gives a nominal mass range of about 0.05 to 5M⊙​.
The endpoint luminosity ratio is 108, whereas the inferred mass ratio is about 102, giving L∝M4 across that range. The exponent is therefore consistent at this schematic level. The solar normalization and individual endpoint masses are much less reliable: using the luminosity relation itself gives approximately 0.1 to 10M⊙​. Central temperatures are not truly constant, low-mass stellar structure differs, and the uncorrected V luminosities in the diagram are not bolometric. These limitations prevent treating the rough radius-based masses as a contradictory precision measurement.

Solution
Words: 72
c OurBigBook.com
If radiation dominates the central pressure, equate Pc​∼GM∗2​/R∗4​ to aTc4​/3. This gives
R∗​∼(a3G​)1/4Tc​M∗1/2​​.​
(17)
At roughly fixed burning temperature, the corresponding mass-radius scaling is R∗​∝M∗1/2​, rather than the gas-pressure estimate R∗​∝M∗​. Radiation pressure alone does not determine a unique radius at a specified mass: a thermal or nuclear-burning condition is still needed to specify Tc​. The relation is a homology estimate, not a universal exact law for all massive stars.

d

Words: 122 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 122
d OurBigBook.com
The numbered features in the original colour-magnitude diagram have the following interpretation.
  • 1: the main sequence, where core hydrogen fusion supplies the luminosity; stars span a range of masses and effective temperatures.
  • 2: the subgiant region, following core hydrogen exhaustion, with a contracting helium-rich core and increasing hydrogen-shell burning.
  • 3: the red giant branch, with an extended cool envelope and a compact helium core fed by hydrogen-shell burning.
  • 4: the roughly horizontal core-helium-burning branch, or its red-clump part, reached after helium ignition; hydrogen-shell burning can continue outside the core.
  • 5: the white-dwarf cooling sequence, consisting of compact remnants supported mainly by electron degeneracy pressure and radiating stored heat.
Continuous star formation explains the coexistence of newly formed massive main-sequence stars with evolved low-mass remnants; interpreting a single sharp turnoff as the age of a coeval cluster would be inappropriate here.

a OurBigBook.com
At this small redshift, D≃cz/H0​≃20.0 Mpc. The outer angular radius gives Rout​≃Dθ≃21.3 kpc. Approximating the dynamical mass by a spherical equivalent,
Mdyn​(<Rout​)≃GVrot2​Rout​​≃4.9×1011M⊙​.​
(18)
The supplied Tully-Fisher relation gives MV​≃−22.49, and hence LV​≃9.9×1010LV,⊙​. Treating the population as solar-like gives the estimate ΥV​≃1M⊙​/LV,⊙​, so
Mluminous​≃1.0×1011M⊙​.​
(19)
The dynamical estimate exceeds that by about a factor of five; a massive extended dark-matter component is the natural interpretation. Solar-like spectra do not exactly fix the population mass-to-light ratio, and a disk is not spherical, but order-unity corrections do not remove this large outer mass excess under the stated estimate.

Words: 96
b OurBigBook.com
The effective radius is one tenth of the optical outer radius: Re​≃2.13 kpc. A flat rotation speed then gives Mdyn​(<Re​)≃4.9×1010M⊙​. Half the luminosity, with the same mass-to-light ratio, implies Mluminous​(<Re​)≃4.9×1010M⊙​.
The inner mass budget does not require a large dark-matter fraction.​
(20)
The concentration of light into a small fraction of the optical radius suggests a high-surface-brightness, centrally concentrated disk galaxy, plausibly an early-type spiral or lenticular with a substantial bulge. The kinematic and photometric data do not uniquely distinguish those morphologies. Disk geometry, an unknown inclination correction, or a varying stellar mass-to-light ratio would alter the exact numerical inner comparison.

Words: 87
c OurBigBook.com
Using the same luminosity estimate, the distance modulus is 12.5−(−22.49)=34.99, implying D≃99.4 Mpc. Pure Hubble expansion at that distance predicts about 7450kms−1. The measured velocity therefore implies
vpec,los​≃6500−7450≃−950kms−1.​
(21)
Its line-of-sight peculiar velocity is toward us, of the order expected for orbital motions in a rich galaxy cluster. A galaxy falling toward a cluster centre from its far side could have this sign. Its actual front/back location or three-dimensional orbit is not determined without the cluster's mean velocity, distance and projected position. Tully-Fisher scatter and the assumption of identical luminosities also limit that inference.

d OurBigBook.com
Let I denote a characteristic surface brightness and Υ=M/L the relevant dynamical mass-to-light ratio. With comparable profiles, L∝IR2 and M∝V2R/G. Eliminating R gives
L∝G2Υ2IV4​.​
(22)
If both I and Υ are independent of speed, converting luminosity to magnitude gives MV​=constant−10log10​V. The empirical coefficient −8 instead means L∝V3.2, and therefore
Υ2I∝V0.8.​
(23)
For constant surface brightness this requires Υ∝V0.4; for constant mass-to-light ratio it requires I∝V0.8. A mixture of these changes, including varying stellar populations or dark-matter fractions, can give the same observed slope. The simple derivation assumes comparable characteristic radii and structural coefficients.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
The curvature constant specifies the intrinsic spatial curvature of homogeneous constant-time slices. Positive curvature has spherical geometry, zero curvature Euclidean geometry, and negative curvature hyperbolic geometry. A conventional coordinate normalization uses k=+1,0,−1, with the scale factor carrying the curvature radius; rescaling that factor changes the numerical magnitude assigned to a dimensional curvature coefficient.
The sign alone does not determine the future expansion once a cosmological constant is admitted. Nor does negative or zero local curvature by itself determine the global topology: quotient spaces can share the same local curvature.

Solution
Words: 76
b OurBigBook.com
For conserved nonrelativistic matter, ρM​=ρM0​a−3, where a=R/R0​ and a0​=1. Substitution into the Friedmann equation gives
H2=H02​(ΩM​a−3+Ωk​a−2+ΩΛ​),
(24)
with
ΩM​=3H02​8πGρM0​​,Ωk​=−H02​R02​kc2​,ΩΛ​=3H02​Λ​.​
(25)
The source writes the dimensionless normalized factor as R in its final expression; this is equivalent to setting R0​=1 consistently in the curvature coefficient. Evaluating today gives ΩM​+Ωk​+ΩΛ​=1. Here the printed Λ already has dimensions of inverse time squared. If the cosmological constant is instead defined geometrically with inverse-length-squared units, replace this Λ by Λgeom​c2.

c

Words: 154 Articles: 1
3 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 154
c OurBigBook.com
With zero curvature and no cosmological constant, the present normalization requires ΩM​=1. Thus a˙=H0​a−1/2, and choosing the big bang as t=0 gives
a(t)=(23H0​t​)2/3,t0​=3H0​2​.​
(26)
For an empty expanding model, Ωk​=1 and the curvature must be negative. The equation becomes a˙=H0​, giving
a(t)=H0​t,t0​=H0−1​.​
(27)
The latter is the Milne slicing of flat spacetime; its zero-scale-factor origin is not a matter-density curvature singularity. In the matter model, gravity decelerates expansion, so the earlier slope was greater than the present slope and the same present size was reached in less time. With the stipulated H0​, the two model ages are approximately 8.69 and 13.0 Gyr.

d

Words: 144 Articles: 1
3 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 144
d OurBigBook.com
Adiabatic photon redshifting gives T∝a−1. Using the stipulated temperatures,
1+zrec​≃1000,zrec​≃999.​
(28)
In the flat dust approximation of part c, t=t0​a3/2, so trec​≃(2/3H0​)1000−3/2≃2.75×105 years. This approximation omits the significant radiation contribution near the actual recombination epoch.
The elementary travel-distance estimate is ctrec​≃8.4×104 pc, whose corresponding comoving scale today is about 84 Mpc. In an expanding universe, however, that is not the exact proper particle-horizon radius. Integrating the null geodesic gives
dhor​(t)=a(t)c∫0t​a(t′)dt′​=3ct
(29)
for dust. Thus the proper horizon at this epoch is about 0.25 Mpc and its present comoving size about 250 Mpc. The factor three accounts for expansion during light propagation. These scales describe the limited causal domain in the simple decelerating model. The near-uniform CMB temperature across much more widely separated last-scattering regions motivates the horizon problem; the question's rough ct estimate and the exact dust horizon should not be conflated.

Solution
Words: 60
a OurBigBook.com
The de Broglie hypothesis associates a wave phase with a material particle. Its momentum and energy set
λ=ph​,ω=ℏE​,k=ℏp​.​
(30)
This is not a literal extended classical lump of matter oscillating at every point. A wavefunction gives amplitudes for measurements, and a localized particle is represented by a superposition of momentum waves. Electron diffraction, for example, exhibits interference at angles set by the same wavelength relation.

b

Words: 74 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 74
b OurBigBook.com
Using the given one-component equipartition estimate, p2=MkB​T. Substituting into the de Broglie relation gives
λ(T)≃MkB​T​h​.​
(31)
Comparison with a confinement length or interparticle spacing d gives the criterion T≲h2/(MkB​d2). Numerical factors depend on the convention: the statistical thermal de Broglie wavelength is usually h/2πMkB​T​, while a three-component root-mean-square momentum introduces a factor 3​. The question's specified one-component convention is used consistently here. Once degeneracy becomes important, classical equipartition itself ceases to describe the electrons accurately.

c

Words: 47 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 47
c OurBigBook.com
Set λ≃d with the convention of part b. Then
Te​≃me​kB​d2h2​≃3.9×105K.​
(32)
Thus ordinary solid-state temperatures are far below this rough overlap scale. The electrons need quantum statistics and quantum states throughout that regime. The number is an order-of-magnitude wavelength criterion, not an exact Fermi temperature: electron density, electronic band structure, effective mass and the numerical convention all matter.

d

Words: 71 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 71
d OurBigBook.com
At the same temperature, momenta increase as the square root of mass, so wavelengths decrease as its inverse square root. For a nucleus of mass MN​≃Amp​,
λe​λN​​=MN​me​​​≃1836A​1​.​
(33)
At the electron overlap threshold, λe​=d, the nuclear wavelength is about 7.0pm/A​, far below the 0.3 nm spacing. Nuclear exchange effects are consequently much less important than electron exchange effects. This statement about nuclear overlap does not mean lattice vibrations are always classical.

e

Words: 122 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 122
e OurBigBook.com
At room temperature, electrons require quantum mechanics, including their occupied orbitals or bands and Fermi statistics. Heavy nuclei can often be treated as distinguishable particles near classical equilibrium lattice sites, because their exchange wavelengths are short. Their coupled displacements form phonons, however, and the occupation of a vibrational mode is classical only if kB​T≫ℏω for that mode. Even at room temperature some high-frequency modes remain quantum mechanical.
At 1 K, quantum lattice vibrations, zero-point motion and the scarcity of thermally excited phonons are essential. Many heavy nuclei still do not have overlapping exchange wavefunctions; quantum vibration and quantum exchange are distinct criteria. For the same spacing, the nuclear overlap threshold from the rough estimate is TN​≃211/A K, illustrating why the nuclear mass cannot be omitted from a blanket low-temperature claim.

Quantum tunnelling is transmission through a region where the particle's energy is below the classical potential energy. The stationary wavefunction decays within that region but need not vanish at its far boundary, so matching can leave a nonzero transmitted probability current.
This does not require a particle to borrow energy temporarily. Energy is conserved for a time-independent barrier; the classically forbidden region is described by an evanescent wave, with the same stationary energy as the incident and transmitted waves.

Matching contributes a prefactor, so this exponential approximation is not an exact transmission coefficient for a transparent or very thin barrier. For two moving particles the relative-coordinate mass is their reduced mass.

Solution

Two major suppressions are missing from the one-femtometre rectangular estimate. First, the Coulomb barrier extends far beyond nuclear distances and is not rectangular. A semiclassical integral through it produces the Gamow factor exp(−2πη), with η=αfs​μc2/(2E)​; at the illustrative thermal energy it is already of order 10−11. A thermal average additionally weights the high-energy tail and is not the same as evaluating a single thermal energy.
Second, two protons cannot simply form a stable bound diproton. The proton–proton chain starts with a weak-interaction conversion producing a deuteron, a Positron and a neutrino. The weak transition probability supplies a further very large suppression. Thus the quoted tiny fusion probability is not a pure one-dimensional barrier transmission probability with universal energy-independent meaning.
The Sun contains of order 1057 nucleons in a hot dense core and offers enormously many encounters over astronomical times. A very small reaction probability per encounter can therefore supply its luminosity while consuming only a small fraction of the fuel per unit time. The small weak reaction rate is also crucial for the long stellar lifetime; a larger core temperature increases burning and triggers expansion and cooling.

The Shockley-Queisser calculation treats a single-junction solar cell with a single band gap, in steady state, with one collected electron-hole pair per absorbed above-gap photon, an ideal absorption edge, thermalized carriers and radiative recombination as the limiting recombination process. The source spectrum, cell temperature, angular acceptance and optical concentration must be specified. Below-gap photons are transmitted; energy above the gap is lost during carrier thermalization; the cell must emit photons by detailed balance, producing a recombination current and an entropy-related voltage loss. Delivering power at finite current also puts the operating voltage below the open-circuit voltage. Nonradiative recombination, resistance and imperfect collection worsen a real cell but are not required for the ideal limit.
Three ways to change those assumptions are tandem solar cells, which divide the spectrum among gaps and reduce both transmission and thermalization losses; hot-carrier solar cells, which aims to collect excess carrier energy before thermalization; and carrier multiplication or spectral conversion, which aims to use a high-energy photon for more than one excitation or combine otherwise unusable sub-gap photons. These concepts have additional practical losses and do not automatically outperform an optimized conventional device. The usual unconcentrated single-junction optimum is approximately one third under a terrestrial solar spectrum, rather than a universal efficiency independent of illumination.
For the geometrical estimate, take the stated horizontal equinox irradiance to set a constant direct-normal reference. The equinox solar-noon elevation is αe​=90∘−51.75∘=38.25∘, so this reference is In​=1/sinαe​≃1.62kWm−2. A south-facing panel with tilt β=41.1∘ has noon incidence factor cos(51.75∘−δ−41.1∘), where δ=±23.44∘. Relative to the 1kWm−2 plane-of-array rating,
PJune​≃5sin38.25∘cos12.79∘​=7.9kW,PDecember​≃5sin38.25∘cos34.09∘​=6.7kW.​
(47)
These are the results of that idealized geometrical normalization, not credible seasonal production forecasts. Its inferred direct-normal irradiance already exceeds the approximately 1.36kWm−2 solar irradiance outside the atmosphere, so the supplied horizontal benchmark cannot describe a purely direct noon beam literally. Real direct and diffuse fractions, atmospheric attenuation at low winter elevation, cell temperature and inverter clipping are unspecified. An alternative assumption of 1kWm−2 direct-normal irradiance gives approximately 4.88 and 4.14 kW. A physically unique maximum cannot be inferred without an irradiance model.
The stated annual output corresponds to 4100/5=820 full-rated hours, an average power of 0.468 kW and a capacity factor of 9.4%. Night, cloud, seasonal day length and other losses explain the large difference from an instantaneous sunlit estimate.
For a national scale estimate, take UK area 2.44×1011m2, population 6.6×107, and annual mean solar input 100Wm−2. Covering five percent with twenty-percent-efficient modules gives
NdayE​∼1000(6.6×107)0.05(2.44×1011)(0.20)(100)(24)​≃89kWhperson−1day−1.​
(48)
This is comparable with an order-100 kWh daily per-person primary-energy budget, and much larger than electricity use alone, of order 10-15 kWh per person per day. It is a gross area-and-flux estimate: access land, shading, seasonal storage, curtailment and conversion between primary energy and electrical end use all affect its interpretation.

A pumped-storage plant moves water uphill using electrical power, then returns it through a turbine and generator when electricity is needed. The upper and lower reservoirs set the usable volume and head; pumps, penstocks, valves and reversible pump-turbines set the power and flow. The plant stores energy rather than generating net energy over a cycle.
For constant head, the gravitational energy is Eg​=ρVgh. With the stated generation efficiency,
Eusable​=0.89(1000)(1.4×107)(9.81)(400)≃4.89×1013J=13.6GWh.​
(49)
At 3 GW, P=ηρgQh gives
Q≃8.59×102m3s−1,tfull​=Eusable​/P≃4.53h.​
(50)
Head variation, dead volume and hydraulic losses beyond the stipulated efficiency have been neglected.
To deliver 9 kWh with the same head and efficiency needs V≃9.3m3 of water, roughly a 2.1 m cube, together with a 400 m elevation difference and a lower reservoir. At a 10 m head it would need about 370m3. This contrasts with the small fuel volume: the useful energy density of lifted water depends on its external head, not its chemical composition.
Pumped storage offers long service life, fast dispatch, substantial power, and separate choices of storage volume and turbine rating. Its drawbacks include geographic constraints, construction cost and time, ecological impacts, evaporation and water requirements, plus round-trip losses. The quoted generation efficiency alone is not the round-trip efficiency because pumping also consumes more than the stored potential energy.
The rock cylinder has mass ρr​πr2(2r) and rises through r. Equating its useful energy to the reservoir result cancels the common efficiency and gravity:
2πρr​r4=ρw​Vh,r=[2π(3000)1000(1.4×107)(400)​]1/4≃131m.​
(51)
Its height is about 262 m and its lift about 131 m, ignoring buoyancy as instructed. Stored energy scales as r4, excavated volume roughly as r3, and lined area as r2. If excavation dominates cost, cost per unit stored energy decreases approximately as r−1. Seals, increasing pressure, geology, leakage, supporting structure and power equipment can change that scaling; a volume law is not a complete cost model.

Solution
Words: 200
a OurBigBook.com
Fission divides a heavy nucleus into more tightly bound fragments, releasing energy through the increase in binding energy per nucleon. A neutron-induced chain reaction can sustain heat production in a controlled reactor. Fusion combines light nuclei into more tightly bound products and needs sufficiently high temperature and confinement to obtain a useful reaction rate despite Coulomb repulsion. Both ultimately supply heat that must be converted to electricity, unless a different energy-conversion scheme is explicitly introduced.
A typical fission releases about 200 MeV per event, corresponding to roughly 8×1013 J per kilogram of fully fissioned heavy fuel. The deuterium-tritium fusion energy of 17.6 MeV per reaction corresponds to about 3.4×1014 J per kilogram of reacting mixture. These are nuclear reaction energies, not electricity per kilogram of mined or engineered fuel. Actual fuel use, thermal efficiency, parasitic power and incomplete burn change plant output.
Fission has substantial operating experience and can provide high-capacity-factor generation, but faces capital, waste, decommissioning, fuel-cycle and safety constraints. Fusion avoids a self-sustaining neutron chain reaction in the fuel, but its systems still face neutron damage, activated materials, tritium management and demanding heat extraction. Demonstrating a hot plasma or a favorable reaction-energy balance is not the same as demonstrating economical net electricity. The useful comparison distinguishes scientific feasibility, engineering availability and whole-system cost.

b

Words: 198 Articles: 1
3 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 198
b OurBigBook.com
Distributed generation changes the shape of infrastructure rather than eliminating it. A 1 GW power station is large, but supplying a national mean demand of tens of gigawatts from smaller intermittent generators still requires transmission, distribution, power conversion, forecasting, balancing and often storage or dispatchable reserve. Geographic diversity can reduce weather correlations only if power can move between regions.
For scale, delivering 30 GW through a network is a continuous transfer of 30 billion joules each second. Even a distributed average installation of 3 kW per household needs ten million participating households to reach that power, before allowing for capacity factor. Solar roofs can reduce some local flows while export peaks or winter deficits increase others. District heat, offshore wind connections, interconnectors and fuel transport also have economies of scale.
Large centralized assets can introduce single-point failure, slow construction and financing risk; modular systems can be installed incrementally and offer local control. Conversely, network reinforcement and seasonal adequacy cannot be inferred from the size of an individual panel. A defensible conclusion is that an effective mix may combine small generators with large shared infrastructure. The categorical claim that large-scale infrastructure has become obsolete does not follow from the existence of distributed generation.

c OurBigBook.com
Compare average delivered electrical power per land area with consistent boundaries. Illustrative values are about 1000Wm−2 for the compact plant site of nuclear generation, 5-15Wm−2 for a UK ground-mounted photovoltaic site, 1-3Wm−2 across a wind-farm lease area, around 0.5Wm−2 for an energy crop after conversion, and perhaps 5Wm−2 for a reservoir hydroelectric scheme. These are scale estimates, not universal technology constants.
At representative values 1000,10,2,0.5,5Wm−2, one average gigawatt requires approximately 1,100,500,2000,200km2 respectively. Biomass therefore has substantial land competition even when fuel can be stored. Solar development competes less with farming if placed on roofs or already developed land. Wind's large separation area is not entirely excluded from agriculture; its actual foundations and roads occupy a much smaller area. Reservoir impacts can be extensive and strongly site dependent.
A nuclear-site number excludes mining, cooling constraints, transport and exclusion areas; a wind lease number includes much land still usable for other purposes. Reporting them as identical measures of permanently occupied land would mislead. Deployment decisions need both the average energy yield and the consequences of the particular land boundary, ecology, food production and local acceptance.

Words: 190 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 190
d OurBigBook.com
A battery stores electrochemical free energy. Representative pack specific energy is of order 0.1-0.25 kWh/kg, with electrical round-trip efficiency roughly 85-95%. It responds rapidly and can be modular, but energy capacity requires more active material, and ageing depends on time, temperature and cycling.
Pumped storage stores gravitational potential energy. At a 400 m head with 89% generation efficiency, useful energy is ηgh≃0.97 Wh/kg of water. Its low mass-specific energy is acceptable when inexpensive water and large reservoirs are available. Storage volume and generator rating can be chosen substantially independently, making multi-hour service practical, but suitable sites and civil works are major constraints.
Hydrogen stores chemical energy, with a lower heating value around 33 kWh/kg of hydrogen before allowing for tank mass. Electrolysis, compression or other storage processing, and conversion back to electricity can reduce electrical round-trip efficiency to roughly 25-45%, depending on the route. Separate tanks or caverns can make long-duration energy capacity less expensive than adding electrochemical cells, but containment, infrastructure, leakage and conversion equipment matter.
The appropriate comparison includes power rating, energy duration, cycle count, system mass or area, and whether heat or electricity is the final useful product. A large fuel heating value does not imply a high electricity-storage efficiency.

An experience curve models unit cost as C(Q)=C0​(Q/Q0​)−b, where Q is cumulative production. A doubling reduces cost by a fraction 1−2−b. For an illustrative twenty-percent reduction per doubling, b=−log2​(0.8)≃0.322, so four doublings would reduce the fitted cost to 0.84≃0.41 of its initial value.
Photovoltaic modules are manufactured in large numbers with repeated designs, so manufacturing yield, scale, automation and material use can all produce observable learning. Wind turbines also benefit from repeated manufacture, but installation, foundations, access, grid connection and site quality form a larger project-specific share; moving into poorer or more difficult sites may offset improvements. Nuclear reactors have fewer repetitions, long project times, changing designs and regulation, and substantial site and financing costs. A cumulative-capacity curve can therefore hide rather than explain changes in nuclear project cost.
A experience curve is an empirical conditional relationship, not a physical law guaranteeing success. Input prices, policy, financing, saturation of a manufacturing improvement and the definition of system boundary all affect extrapolation. Declining cost may encourage deployment, which then increases the cumulative-production variable, so correlation alone does not establish a one-way causal effect. Forecasts should test multiple learning rates and distinguish module or turbine cost from the cost of a reliable delivered electricity system.

Δc≃3×1011kWh£3×109​=£0.01/kWh=1pence/kWh.​

A doubled capital-cost assumption doubles this charge. This estimate counts backup capacity even if it runs rarely, which is why capital rather than fuel can dominate its fixed annual cost.
It is not the total cost of a renewable or gas system. Fuel, emissions, maintenance, staffing, gas supply during correlated cold weather, network capacity, startup constraints and reliability standards remain additional considerations. Backup requirements need not equal the sum of intermittent nameplate ratings; demand correlation, capacity credit, interconnection and storage matter. The arithmetic shows that a large reserve power rating can have a modest annualized capital charge per unit of total electricity, while leaving substantial practical and environmental constraints unresolved.

1 OurBigBook.com
A strong explanation treats instruments and mathematical descriptions as mutually reinforcing. New instruments expanded the phenomena available for investigation, while mathematical models determined what could be inferred from their readings. Neither a list of inventions nor an account of abstract ideas alone explains the Scientific Revolution.
The telescope changed astronomy by making lunar surface relief, Jupiter's satellites and the phases of Venus observable. Galileo Galilei's observations challenged a sharp physical separation between perfect heavens and an imperfect Earth and showed that not every celestial motion was centred on Earth. The full range of Venusian phases contradicted the traditional Ptolemaic arrangement, but could also fit a geoheliocentric model: the observation did not by itself uniquely prove a moving Earth. Interpreting an unfamiliar optical image required repeated observations, comparison between instruments and a convincing account of optical reliability.[ref]
Quantitative mechanics also depended on measurement: controlled motion experiments, timing, balances and geometrical reconstruction made relationships such as distance proportional to elapsed-time squared testable. Johannes Kepler used precise positional astronomy to replace uniform circular combinations by mathematical laws of planetary motion. Isaac Newton then linked terrestrial falling and celestial orbits through common dynamical laws and universal gravitation. This was more than fitting curves: a small mathematical framework connected otherwise disparate phenomena and generated further predictions.
The air pump, barometer and improved thermometry similarly turned pressure and atmospheric effects into reproducible laboratory subjects. Robert Boyle's pressure-volume relation exemplifies how an engineered apparatus and quantitative regularity could develop together. Such experiments required skilled craft, calibration, environmental control and credible witnesses, not merely a solitary theorist manipulating symbols.
Mathematization was therefore transformative because it replaced many qualitative classifications with quantities, relations and calculable idealizations. It was selective: a frictionless body or point mass is not an immediate sensory object, and an effective model can abstract from the very imperfections an instrument reveals. Instruments made those abstractions answerable to new evidence. Printing, patronage, observatories, correspondence and learned societies helped stabilize results across different observers. The best assessment gives neither instruments nor mathematics exclusive causal priority; their interaction, within these social arrangements, produced a new style of explanation and evidence.

2

Words: 374 Articles: 1
S14 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 374
2 OurBigBook.com
Eighteenth-century support for the Newtonian system accumulated through successful predictions, the resolution of apparent discrepancies and increasingly precise terrestrial tests. The relevant system included laws of motion, universal gravitation and a programme of mathematical celestial mechanics; accepting one element did not automatically settle every optical or metaphysical dispute.
Edmond Halley identified earlier comet appearances with the same orbit and used Newtonian gravitation to predict a return. Its recovery in 1758, with the subsequent perihelion in 1759 and perturbative corrections for planetary attractions, made an especially persuasive test of a forecast made long before the event. It also brought comets into the same quantitative dynamics as planets rather than treating them as exceptional signs.[ref]
Geodetic expeditions compared meridian arcs at different latitudes. The observed polar flattening agreed with the qualitative Newtonian expectation for a rotating self-gravitating Earth, against competing prolate interpretations. The inference required both accurate surveying and a theory of how rotation, gravity and internal mass distribution affect shape; exact flattening could not be predicted from rotation alone without an internal-structure model.[ref]
Lunar and planetary perturbation theory provided a sustained, more demanding test than unperturbed Keplerian ellipses. Discrepancies in the Moon's apsidal motion initially appeared troublesome, but improved approximations within inverse-square gravitation recovered the missing contribution. Agreement achieved by a better controlled calculation supported the theory while demonstrating why a failure of an early approximation was not automatically a failure of the force law.
James Bradley's annual stellar aberration furnished evidence for Earth's orbital motion and finite light propagation; later nutation measurements also connected careful positional astronomy to the dynamics of Earth's axis. Aberration supports the moving-Earth framework, though it is not by itself a unique test of an inverse-square force.[ref]
Finally, Henry Cavendish's torsion-balance experiment in 1798 measured attraction between laboratory masses and inferred Earth's mean density. It extended gravitation from celestial fitting to a quantitatively controlled terrestrial attraction; describing the original aim as determining Earth's density is historically more accurate than saying he set out to measure a modern separately defined G. Together these tests supplied converging support across scales. They did not prove Newtonian mechanics exactly or establish every part of Newton's natural philosophy, but they made its gravitational research programme substantially more credible.

Words: 359 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 359
3 OurBigBook.com
Michael Faraday established new electrical phenomena through carefully varied experiments and made the field a central explanatory concept. His achievements were not confined to a single apparatus or to applications later expressed in equations by other researchers.
In 1821 he demonstrated continuous electromagnetic rotation: a current-carrying conductor could move around a magnet, or a magnet around a conductor, with the current maintained through an appropriate contact. The circular motion was difficult to reduce to an ordinary static attraction along a line and provided an experimental route toward electric-motor action.
In 1831 his induction experiments linked changing magnetic conditions to an induced electrical response. In the ring-coil arrangement, switching current in one winding produced a transient deflection in the other winding rather than a persistent response to a steady current. Moving a magnet relative to a coil produced a related effect. Comparing these arrangements helped identify change of magnetic linkage, rather than mere proximity to a magnet, as the essential feature. His rotating-disc generator showed a further way to obtain electrical output from mechanical motion.[ref]
His electrolysis studies established quantitative relationships between charge transferred and material deposited or liberated. These supported a connection between chemical change and definite electrical quantities, even though they did not yet amount to a modern atomic theory of charge. His work on dielectrics and electrostatic shielding examined how materials and conducting boundaries influence electrical effects.
In 1845 he observed magnetic rotation of the plane of polarization in a material and investigated diamagnetism. The magneto-optical effect gave experimental evidence for a connection between light and magnetism, while diamagnetism showed a response opposite to ordinary magnetic attraction. Those findings broadened electromagnetism beyond currents and permanent magnets.[ref]
Faraday's lines of force emphasized processes in the intervening region rather than only direct action at a distance. James Clerk Maxwell subsequently converted crucial parts of that field conception into a mathematical electromagnetic theory. Calling Faraday merely an unmathematical precursor would miss the explanatory and experimental content of his field ideas; crediting him with Maxwell's completed equations would be equally inaccurate. His legacy combines new effects, reproducible experimental techniques, quantitative electrochemistry and a fertile physical picture of fields.

Solution

Words: 367
4 OurBigBook.com
Energy conservation is a strong example of convergent discovery in the 1840s, but only if “simultaneous” means overlapping contributions rather than identical statements made at the same instant. Different researchers reached related conclusions from physiology, engineering, electricity and mechanics, with different evidence and terminology.
Julius Robert Mayer argued in 1842 for an indestructible, interconvertible agency underlying natural processes and related mechanical work to heat using thermal properties of gases. His physiological motivations and theoretical reasoning differed from a direct precision measurement of a mechanical equivalent. James Prescott Joule investigated electrical heating and mechanical production of heat, including fluid-friction experiments. By comparing measured work with measured temperature rises, he supplied increasingly persuasive numerical evidence that a reproducible quantity of work corresponded to a quantity of heat. His later paper describes controls on thermometers and different working fluids, showing that the result depended on experimental metrology, not simply the observation that friction warms things.[ref]
Ludvig Colding pursued related mechanical and thermal ideas and experiments in the same decade. Hermann von Helmholtz's 1847 synthesis connected the impossibility of perpetual motion with the interrelation of mechanical, thermal, electrical and physiological processes. These contributions shared a broad conservation programme without having identical conceptual foundations. A modern historian must also distinguish an invariant quantity, its numerical equivalence across processes, and the general claim that the conservation applies to all physical processes.[ref]
The convergence was historically intelligible. Engines made the relation of heat to work economically important; electrical experiments revealed conversions between previously separate domains; physiology raised questions about animal heat and mechanical effort. Measurement practices and interrelated scientific communities supplied common problems. Earlier work on frictional heating and mechanical conservation provided resources, while the caloric account of heat and uncertainty about reversible heat engines remained obstacles.
The differences also limit a simple multiple-discovery story. Recognition was uneven, communication changed later formulations, and priority disputes retrospectively compressed a developing research programme into a single discovery. The first law's mature formulation required further clarification of internal energy, heat and work. Energy conservation is therefore simultaneously an example of independent convergence, cumulative experimental confirmation and later conceptual unification; assigning the entire achievement to one person or saying everyone discovered precisely the same law would conceal that process.

5

Words: 375 Articles: 1
S14 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 375
5 OurBigBook.com
American Big science emerged when expensive instruments and team-based research met unusually strong financial, industrial and political support. Its prehistory matters: the Second World War accelerated an existing development rather than creating large laboratories from nothing.
Ernest Lawrence's prewar cyclotron programme illustrates the instrumental pressure toward scale. Increasing accelerator size demanded magnets, power supplies, vacuum engineering, technical staff and coordinated fundraising. A laboratory could become an organization supporting shared machinery, rather than a professor and a few assistants using tabletop apparatus. Philanthropic and university support helped establish this model before sustained federal patronage expanded it.[ref]
The war then made coordinated scientific work a national priority. Radar and nuclear programmes demonstrated that physicists, engineers, industry and government could combine resources on a scale unavailable to ordinary academic departments. Wartime urgency reduced normal budget constraints and established contractual relationships, facilities and managerial experience. Nuclear weapons added a particularly powerful strategic justification for maintaining those capacities after the war, but should not be taken as the sole origin of large-scale research.
Postwar institutions converted emergency mobilization into durable support. National laboratories provided expensive shared facilities; defense agencies supported research and training; universities expanded; and national prestige became tied to scientific capability. Vannevar Bush's 1945 report argued for continued public support of basic research and scientific talent, while also defending investigator freedom. It was an influential programme for the government-university relationship, not a claim that all research should be centrally directed through enormous projects.[ref]
Cold War competition reinforced funding for accelerators, space research, computing and other large undertakings. The United States combined a large industrial economy, relatively intact postwar infrastructure and an expanded university system, making that commitment feasible at an especially high level. The dependence on federal budgets also brought secrecy, strategic priorities and vulnerability to political changes.
Big science did not make small experiments or individual theoretical work obsolete. Large facilities can answer otherwise inaccessible questions, but coordination costs, long lead times and concentration of resources can narrow the available research portfolio. The timing is best explained by the interaction of scientific instrument requirements, prewar organizational experiments, wartime mobilization and sustained postwar state patronage, rather than by an inevitable internal law that every science must simply become larger.

for every component. This is the Klein-Gordon equation. Its componentwise satisfaction is a necessary consequence of the first-order Dirac equation, not a converse selecting all spinor solutions of the squared equation.

A two-dimensional representation is impossible: all four matrices α1​,α2​,α3​,β would be traceless 2×2 matrices. Anticommutation gives Tr(AB)=0 for distinct matrices, whereas Tr(A2)=2. They would therefore be four linearly independent members of the three-dimensional complex space of traceless 2×2 matrices, a contradiction.
N is even and N≥4.​

The usual irreducible 3+1 dimensional Dirac representation has N=4. Larger representations can contain multiple copies; the requested lower bound is not itself a proof of irreducibility.

This follows from the radiation-integral expression εx0​=Cq​γ2I5​/(Jx​I2​): at fixed optical phase advance the dispersion-invariant scaling makes the ratio proportional to the cube of the cell bend.

The accelerating supply transfers Ie​V=50 kW into the beam, but the electrons need not be discarded with that kinetic energy. An electrostatic recovery system decelerates the used beam before collection and returns most of its energy to the electric field or supply. The net required power then covers unrecovered beam energy and losses, rather than the whole circulating kinetic-energy flux.
For example, 99% recovery leaves 0.01(50kW)≃500 W of unrecovered beam power, plus auxiliary loads. This explains the stated two-order-of-magnitude scale. It does not imply that gun heating, vacuum equipment, magnets and all electrical losses are automatically included in a 500 W total plant budget.

Regenerative braking in an electric vehicle converts part of its mechanical kinetic energy back into electrical energy stored in a battery, rather than dissipating it all in friction brakes. An industrial recuperative heat exchanger transfers heat from a hot exhaust stream to incoming process fluid, reducing the required new heat input.
Both recover energy that would otherwise be rejected, while remaining subject to conversion losses and limits on the usefulness of the recovered form. Neither is a source of net energy over a complete cycle.

Express temperatures as energies Θ=kB​T. A longitudinal cathode-energy spread of order Θc​ remains of that order during an ideal common electrostatic acceleration. At final mean speed v0​, a small energy spread produces δv∥​≃δE/(me​v0​). In the accompanying beam frame, the corresponding random kinetic-energy scale is
Θ∥​∼2me​δv∥2​​∼2me​v02​Θc2​​=4Ee​Θc2​​​.

The last equality uses the nonrelativistic acceleration energy Ee​=me​v02​/2. This is the approximate temperature convention supplied in the hint; exact numerical factors depend on the emitted distribution and the definition of spread. At 50 keV, relativistic corrections are modest but not strictly zero.
Electrostatic acceleration narrows longitudinal velocity spread relative to the fast mean beam even though it does not remove each electron's transverse cathode motion. In ideal magnetized cooling, slow proton motion couples to the electron guiding-centre dynamics, making this very small longitudinal spread relevant to the attainable ion temperature. Practical voltage ripple, space charge, alignment errors and ion heating can set much larger limits.

Θ⊥​≃Θc​.​

More generally the magnetic moment of the orbit gives Θ⊥​/B≃constant, so the equality assumes the same relevant field strength, not merely that a field is present all along the line.
In the strong-magnetization regime, many electron gyro-orbits occur during an important long-range electron-ion interaction and the gyroradius is small. The ion then interacts predominantly with a guiding centre; rapid transverse cyclotron motion does not act like an unmagnetized bath at the full transverse electron temperature. This allows a proton equilibrium scale far below Tc​ despite the hot transverse gyro-motion.[ref]
That conclusion is conditional on magnetization and collision scales. A finite gyroradius, nonadiabatic fields or transverse beam errors can restore heating and degrade cooling; it is not generally true that transverse temperature can never affect the cooled beam.

A thin spherical shell of thickness dr has mass 4πr2ρdr. Balancing its inward gravitational force with the pressure difference across its faces gives
drdP​=−r2GMr​ρ​,drdMr​​=4πr2ρ.​
(154)
For a transparent estimate take constant density ρ=3M⊙​/(4πR⊙3​) and negligible surface pressure. Then Mr​=M⊙​r3/R⊙3​, so integration gives
Pc​=8πR⊙4​3GM⊙2​​≃1.3×1014Pa.​
(155)
Combining with the ideal gas law and μ≃0.6 yields Tc​≃μmH​GM⊙​/(2kB​R⊙​)≃7×106 K. The less specific virial scaling gives Tc​∼μmH​GM⊙​/(kB​R⊙​)∼107 K.
The real Sun is strongly centrally concentrated: a uniform-density model substantially underestimates central pressure and is not a detailed solar model. Its value is a justified scale estimate, while more realistic structure produces central temperatures of order 1.5×107 K and central pressures of order 1016 Pa. Hydrostatic equilibrium alone does not uniquely determine both profiles without an equation of state and a density/thermal model.

Words: 234 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 234
b OurBigBook.com
Multiply hydrostatic equilibrium by 4πr3dr and integrate from centre to surface. Integration by parts, neglecting external surface pressure, gives
−3∫PdV=−∫0M​rGMr​​dMr​=Ω.
(156)
For an ideal gas with a constant adiabatic index, U=∫PdV/(γ−1). Consequently
3(γ−1)U+Ω=0.​
(157)
A fully ionized, nonrelativistic monatomic gas has γ=5/3, provided gas rather than radiation or degeneracy dominates the thermal equation of state. It then obeys 2U+Ω=0​ and E=U+Ω=−U=Ω/2.
Added nuclear heat initially raises pressure and causes expansion. The expansion makes gravitational energy less negative and can lower the temperature of the self-gravitating gas, reducing the temperature-sensitive fusion rate. Conversely, a small contraction can raise the core temperature and increase burning. This negative feedback explains stable main-sequence burning in an ordinary nondegenerate stellar core; a degenerate core need not respond the same way.
Before hydrogen ignition, a cloud loses energy by radiation and contracts. Its gravitational energy decreases; for the ideal-gas virial relation, roughly half the released binding energy heats the gas and half is radiated. Heating continues until nuclear reactions can balance the luminosity, explaining the Kelvin-Helmholtz phase of pre-main-sequence evolution.
The effective adiabatic response varies with ionization, molecular dissociation, radiation pressure and degeneracy. Partial ionization can absorb compression energy and lower the local first adiabatic exponent below 4/3, encouraging compressibility, convection and pulsational instability. A local outer layer with γ≤4/3 does not by itself prove global collapse: ordinary stars have ionization layers of that kind. The dynamical stability criterion concerns a suitable pressure-weighted global response and its coupling to the eigenmode; an extended star with an effectively global exponent below 4/3 can be dynamically unstable.

For an illustrative photospheric gas density 3×10−4kgm−3 and mean molecular weight near 1.3, the ideal gas pressure is about 104 Pa. Thus gas pressure dominates those outer layers by many orders of magnitude. Both the temperature and density are needed: low temperature alone is not a complete comparison.
For homologous stars, hydrostatic and ideal-gas estimates give T∼μmH​GM/(kB​R) and ρ∼M/R3. Therefore
Pgas​Prad​​=3ρkB​aμmH​T3​∝μ4M2​,
(158)
with a structural coefficient independent of mass only under the homology assumption. As mass rises, radiation becomes increasingly important. A rough solar interior normalization of 10−3-10−2 suggests equality after a mass increase by tens, while realistic radiation-dominated structure and composition shift the scale; stars of order 102M⊙​ are a useful estimate for strong radiation support. The very small photospheric ratio must not be used as a universal normalization for their whole interiors.
Radiation also transfers outward momentum. Comparing radiative acceleration κL/(4πr2c) with gravity gives the Eddington luminosity
LEdd​=κ4πcGM​.​
(159)
Near this scale, radiatively driven winds and envelope instabilities can remove matter or impede further accretion. Opacity, composition, rotation, mass loss and formation history affect the limiting stellar mass. The Eddington condition is a luminosity-to-mass constraint, not a unique composition-independent maximum stellar mass.

Opacity is the extinction cross section per unit mass for radiation; a frequency-dependent value κν​ gives dIν​/ds=−κν​ρIν​ when emission is considered separately. Stellar radiative diffusion generally uses an appropriately weighted Rosseland mean opacity. The associated local mean free path is of order 1/(κρ).
At sufficiently high temperature the material is highly ionized, and scattering by free electrons is often dominant for ordinary stellar densities and photon energies well below the electron rest energy. Bound-bound and bound-free absorption weaken as bound electrons disappear; free-free absorption can still matter depending on temperature and density. Thus “high temperature” does not fix the dominant opacity at every possible density. The next part explicitly imposes a Kramers absorption law as a separate scaling model.

d OurBigBook.com
Core-helium-burning stars populate the horizontal branch and red clump; hot subdwarf B stars provide examples with a helium-burning core of roughly half a solar mass and a very small remaining hydrogen envelope. Their high luminosity relative to mass, hot spectra and locations away from an ordinary hydrogen-burning main sequence are observational evidence for such evolved configurations.
A plausible history starts with a hydrogen-burning star. After central hydrogen exhaustion, hydrogen-shell burning builds a compact helium core and the envelope expands on the red giant branch. Sufficient core temperature ignites helium, often by a helium flash for a low-mass degenerate core. Strong mass loss or binary interaction can strip most of the hydrogen envelope, exposing a hot helium-burning remnant; retaining a substantial envelope instead gives an ordinary horizontal-branch or red-clump star.
The simple radiative Kramers scaling estimates a luminosity contrast but does not uniquely identify one evolutionary state or predict a real subdwarf luminosity precisely. A similarly low-mass helium white dwarf would be a cooling, degenerate object rather than the sustained high-temperature helium-burning configuration assumed here.

a OurBigBook.com
The sequence primarily orders effective temperature rather than chemical composition. Hot O spectra show strong ionized-helium features and highly ionized metals, with relatively weak neutral-hydrogen lines. B stars show neutral helium and increasingly prominent hydrogen. A stars have the strongest Balmer absorption. Through F and G, lower-ionization metal lines and calcium features become prominent. K stars have strong low-ionization metal absorption and cool-star features; M stars develop strong molecular bands such as TiO, while Balmer absorption is weak.
Line opacity depends on how many atoms occupy both the relevant ionization stage and the particular lower level. Boltzmann excitation controls the latter and Saha ionization the former, so equal elemental abundances need not give equal line strengths. Electron pressure, surface gravity, broadening and atmospheric temperature gradients also affect the spectrum.
For Balmer absorption the lower state is n=2, 10.2 eV above the hydrogen ground state. In cool atmospheres its population is exponentially small. At higher temperatures it rises, but at still higher temperature ionization removes neutral hydrogen. The competition gives the maximum in A-type stars, with effective temperatures around 9000-10,000 K. This is an excitation-and-ionization effect, not evidence that A stars have the largest hydrogen abundance.

Hydrostatic equilibrium means that the local pressure gradient balances gravity, with no large acceleration or strength-supported departure from that balance. In a spherical planet,
drdP​=−ρ(r)r2GM(r)​.​
(173)
Here M(r) is the enclosed mass, not a constant total mass at every interior radius. If composition is uniform and the radial thermodynamic path is adiabatic, the relevant bulk modulus is Ks​=ρ(dP/dρ)s​. The chain rule then gives the Adams-Williamson relation
drdρ​=Ks​ρ​drdP​=−Ks​r2GM(r)ρ2​.​
(174)
A phase transition or composition jump must be treated separately; its density change is not obtained by integrating one smooth homogeneous-adiabatic equation through it.
The seismic parameter is
Φ=VP2​−34​VS2​=ρKs​​,drdρ​=−r2ΦGM(r)ρ​.​
(175)
The shear modulus μ measures resistance to shear deformation. Solids with μ>0 transmit shear waves; an ideal fluid has zero static shear modulus, so it cannot carry a bulk S wave, while compressional P waves can still propagate through its nonzero bulk modulus.
Limitations include uncertain seismic coverage, temperature and composition tradeoffs, nonadiabatic boundary layers, phase changes, lateral heterogeneity, rotation and finite material strength. Small asteroids and comet nuclei commonly retain irregular shapes because their self-gravity is too weak to overcome strength and impact history; a few larger bodies, such as Ceres, are much closer to global hydrostatic figures. A spherical shape alone is not a complete proof of present hydrostatic equilibrium.
Two complementary remote constraints are precise spacecraft tracking, which measures gravitational harmonics and constrains mass distribution when combined with shape and rotation; and tidal or rotational measurements, such as Love numbers, librations and spin precession, which constrain deformability, moment of inertia and possible fluid layers. Magnetic induction measurements in a time-varying external field can provide an additional conductivity constraint, but are not a unique density inversion.
For the June 2018 lunar picture, start with a regolith and fractured crust, a largely anorthositic crust tens of kilometres thick, a silicate mantle, a deep partially molten region and a small iron-rich core. GRAIL and Apollo-based models gave a global mean crustal thickness around 34-43 km.[ref] A representative seismic model has a partial-melt boundary near radius 480 km, a liquid outer-core boundary near 330 km and a solid inner-core radius near 240 km; these are model-dependent radii from the centre, not depths below the surface.[ref]
The long-running Apollo network had only four principal stations on the near side, with poor global coverage and strong scattering in the fractured near-surface material. Far-side structure and weak deep reflected phases were therefore difficult to constrain. The historical date matters: the answer does not import later Mars seismology or later lunar-core refinements into the 2018 premise.

2 OurBigBook.com
Ancient Martian valley networks, lake basins, deltas, rounded or transported sediments and water-altered minerals show that liquid water was once more widespread than the present cold, low-pressure surface permits. Such evidence motivates a denser early atmosphere and different greenhouse conditions. It does not uniquely establish a continuously warm global ocean: episodic warming, local hydrology and several greenhouse compositions are alternatives that must be tested.
Over time, volatile loss to space, declining interior activity and changing surface storage altered the atmosphere. Early intense solar ultraviolet radiation could drive escape of light species; ion pickup, sputtering and photochemical processes removed additional material. Reduced dynamo activity changed solar-wind interaction, while water and carbon-bearing material could also be sequestered in ice, adsorbed material or minerals. Impacts can both remove and deliver volatiles. The balance is not reducible to one process or to the simple assertion that a magnetic field perfectly retains an atmosphere.
Surface ages are estimated mainly by crater size-frequency statistics, calibrated through radiometric ages and an assumed impact history. More heavily cratered ancient highlands and younger, resurfaced volcanic plains demonstrate substantial age differences on Mars. Lunar sample calibration must be transferred cautiously; erosion, burial and secondary craters complicate counting. Martian meteorites and the pre-2018 Curiosity potassium-argon measurement add radiometric constraints, but a mineral age need not equal the age of its final sedimentary deposition.[ref]
Let Σ=Matm​ denote the printed atmospheric mass per area. An impactor's projected area intercepts a column mcol​=πRimp2​Σ. The requested model assigns energy mcol​Vimp2​/2 to atmospheric removal, and equates it to GMMars​MEsc​/RMars​. Thus
MEsc​=2GMMars​πRimp2​ΣVimp2​RMars​​.​
(176)
This uses a thin atmosphere, a uniform column, surface escape energy, complete useful coupling of that column-energy estimate, and negligible radiative or other losses. It is not a general consequence of the impactor's kinetic energy, which would contain the impactor mass instead of the column mass. A realistic shock/escape calculation needs a coupling model, impact geometry and atmospheric structure. The expression is evaluated as the stipulated approximate model.
At one bar, g≃3.71ms−2, so Σ=P/g≃2.69×104kgm−2 and the total atmospheric mass is 4πRMars2​Σ≃3.89×1018 kg. With a radius of 150 km for the stated diameter,
Matmosphere​MEsc​​=8GMMars​RMars​Rimp2​Vimp2​​≃4.38×10−3≃0.44%,​
(177)
corresponding to about 1.7×1016 kg. The pressure cancels from this fractional estimate. Confusing diameter with radius would overestimate it fourfold.
A single such impact therefore does not remove the bulk of the atmosphere in this model. Repeating an identical fractional loss would require roughly 525 such events for ninety-percent removal, before allowing for volatile delivery or geological evolution. Craters and basins show that bombardment was substantial, but their presence does not establish that the necessary net loss occurred. Heavy-isotope enrichment, including argon and hydrogen isotopes, demonstrates selective escape and constrains competing processes. MAVEN had already supplied evidence for substantial space loss by 2017.[ref] These signatures are not uniquely diagnostic of impact erosion, which can be relatively bulk-like; they should not be presented as proof of impact dominance.

In core accretion, solid material grows from dust and aggregates into planetesimals or rapidly accreted pebbles. A sufficiently large core binds an atmosphere; beyond the snow line, additional condensed volatiles aid solid growth. Cooling allows the envelope to contract and acquire more gas. Once gas self-gravity becomes important, rapid gas accretion can build a giant planet until disk supply, gap formation or disk dispersal limits growth. Migration and interactions with other bodies can alter its final orbit.
Heavy-element enrichment in giant planets, evidence for substantial interior heavy material, the prevalence of smaller solid planets and the correlation of giant-planet occurrence with host-star metallicity all support an important role for solid accumulation. They do not uniquely establish one growth pathway. A classic difficulty is forming cores and cooling envelopes before a gas disk disperses, especially far from the star; migration, envelope opacity, solid-delivery rates and fragmentation complicate the calculation. Pebble-assisted growth can change the timescale, and disk gravitational instability remains a distinct possible route in some environments.
Planetary luminosity is the total emitted power. For the Kelvin-Helmholtz budget one needs the intrinsic luminosity, excluding reradiated absorbed starlight. With orbital distance rp​, Bond albedo AB​, solar luminosity L⊙​ and present-like radius RJ​,
Pabs​=(1−AB​)4rp2​L⊙​RJ2​​.
(178)
The given ratio of emitted to absorbed power is 1.67, so Lint​=0.67Pabs​. Using the supplied radius, rp​=5.2 AU and a solar luminosity around 3.8×1026 W gives
Pabs​≃5.1×1017W,Lint​≃3.4×1017W,​
(179)
consistent with the quoted 3.42×1017 W. Taking 1.67Pabs​ as intrinsic power would incorrectly include reradiated sunlight.
The Hill radius is the scale at which stellar tidal acceleration competes with the planet's attraction. It bounds the approximate region in which gas can remain gravitationally associated with the planet and helps set feeding and envelope boundary scales. With a Jupiter mass,
RH​≃5.2AU(3M⊙​MJ​​)1/3≃0.355AU≃5.3×1010m.​
(180)
Using this as the stipulated extended proto-planet radius and the present-like intrinsic luminosity gives
tKH​∼RH​Lint​GMJ2​​≃4.2×108yr.​
(181)
Using the compact present radius instead would give an even longer value, of order 3×1011 years at that same luminosity. Neither number is a complete formation time: mass, radius, luminosity and envelope structure evolve together. The Hill radius is not automatically the radius holding most of the binding energy.
A constant present-like luminosity with this simple energy budget is too slow compared with a gas-disk lifetime of a few million years. At the Hill-radius energy scale, radiating in 3 Myr would require an average intrinsic luminosity of order 5×1019 W, much brighter than the adopted value. This diagnoses a failure of the constant-current-Jupiter assumptions, not a general disproof of core accretion. Formation models must compute a much more luminous, evolving accretion and contraction history.
